thread.title_full: Worcester families join lawsuit alleging segregation in Massachusetts public schools

author: Bay State News
title: Worcester families join lawsuit alleging segregation in Massachusetts public schools
text:
Families and community groups from Worcester are participating in a lawsuit filed on May 20 that accuses the state of Massachusetts of allowing segregation to persist in its public school system.
The lawsuit, brought before Suffolk County Superior Court, claims that the state’s education policies violate constitutional guarantees for equal and adequate education by segregating Black and Latino students. The case is being led by several families from cities across Massachusetts, including Worcester, along with organizations such as Worcester Interfaith and the YWCA of Central Massachusetts. Lawyers for Civil Rights, Brown’s Promise, and WilmerHale represent the plaintiffs.
“Segregation in Massachusetts schools is the predictable result of policies the state has enacted and maintained for years,” Jillian Lenson, a senior attorney at Lawyers for Civil Rights, said. “Our constitution promises every child an equal and adequate education. That promise cannot coexist with a system that isolates Black and Latino students in underresourced districts.”
The complaint argues that local districting practices have resulted in “poor-packing” lower-income Black and brown students into specific schools with fewer resources. According to a 2024 study from the Racial Imbalance Advisory Council of the state education department, 63% of schools in Massachusetts are classified as “segregated” or “intensely segregated,” meaning non-white students make up at least 90% of enrollment.
“Massachusetts has long held itself out as a leader in public education, but for far too long Black and Latino students across the commonwealth have not been afforded equal access to high-quality schools,” GeDá Jones Herbert, chief legal counsel at Brown’s Promise, said. “The state has a constitutional duty to provide an adequate and equal education to every child in its care. Our clients’ paramount concern is to dismantle the current two-tiered, segregated system, to ensure that all children can learn and thrive together in well-resourced schools.”
In Worcester specifically, data show that 64% of all students identify as students of color; Hispanic students account for nearly 46%. At Doherty Memorial High School—the high school with the lowest percentage—68% identify as minority; North High School has an even higher percentage at 85%. Deborah Hall, CEO of YWCA Central Massachusetts said: “YWCA Central Massachusetts stands with students, families and partners across the Commonwealth to demand equitable, inclusive public education for every child… This lawsuit seeks accountability and strives to create transformative change… ensuring all students are valued, supported and empowered to succeed.”
Defendants named include the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE), Commissioner Pedro Martinez, members of its board as well as other officials. In response DESE stated: “The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education believes that all students… deserve schools where they are known [and] valued… We are committed to building on this progress.” The agency also noted it does not control district boundaries or funding formulas; those decisions rest with local districts or legislators.
Plaintiffs suggest remedies such as expanding vocational programs serving multiple districts or increasing magnet school offerings along with free transportation options so more children can attend different schools outside their home districts.
summary: Families and community groups from Worcester are participating in a lawsuit filed on May 20 that accuses the state of Massachusetts of allowing segregation to persist in its public school system. “Segregation in Massachusetts schools is the predictable result of policies the state has enacted and maintained for years,” Jillian Lenson, a senior attorney at Lawyers for Civil Rights, said.
